screens.title: Forwarding (Bypassing) and Hazard Detection
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we study forwarding, also called bypassing, and the hazard logic that makes it work. Forwarding is the technique that lets an instruction use a result before that result is written back to the register file. That simple idea reduces pipeline stalls dramatically in an in-order five-stage pipeline. You will see the three forwarding paths commonly implemented, the multiplexers that choose forwarded data instead of the register file, and the comparator logic the hazard unit uses to decide when to forward. We will also cover the key exception — the load-use hazard — which cannot be eliminated by forwarding and requires a one-cycle stall. Along the way you will learn why the unit prioritizes the more recent pipeline stage when both stages could forward, and how forwarding changes typical CPI numbers for realistic code. This chapter is practical: it prepares you to design the forwarding multiplexers and the hazard detection logic, to detect load-use cases, and to reason about where stalls remain. Think about forwarding as express highways that let values bypass the register file and arrive at the ALU earlier. Why is that optimization so important in pipelined processors?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Forwarding & Hazard Detection
Forwarding (Bypassing)
Use results before they reach the register file to avoid RAW stalls
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Why it matters
Reduces stall cycles and improves CPI for typical workloads.
Where it acts
At ALU inputs via multiplexers selecting EX/MEM or MEM/WB data.
Key exception
Load-use hazards still require a one-cycle stall.
In this lesson
You will design forwarding selects, write hazard detection conditions, and reason about performance trade-offs.
Explore key topics
Three compact previews below prepare you to build the unit and measure its impact.
Forwarding Paths
EX/MEM→EX, MEM/WB→EX, MEM/WB→MEM
Hazard Logic
Comparators produce select signals for ALU multiplexers.
Load-Use Stall
A load followed by a use requires a single cycle bubble.
Visual concept
Express highways bypass the register file. The hazard control center watches registers and sets multiplexer selects.
Express: EX/MEM → EX
For the immediately preceding instruction.
Fallback: MEM/WB → EX
When the result is from two cycles earlier.
Store case: MEM/WB → MEM
Forwarding data into the memory write input for a store.
Reflection
As you proceed, watch for where forwarding cannot help. That limitation defines compiler and microarchitectural techniques that follow.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement forwarding paths in a five-stage datapath, design the hazard detection unit, explain the load-use limitation, and analyze the performance impact. First, implementing forwarding paths means identifying the ALU inputs that can accept bypassed values and wiring multiplexers to the EX/MEM and MEM/WB pipeline registers. That skill matters because it removes many read-after-write stalls and improves throughput. Second, designing the hazard detection unit requires writing the compare logic that sets those multiplexer selects and enforces priority. Understanding this logic ensures correctness when two previous instructions write the same register. Third, you will learn why forwarding cannot resolve load-use hazards and how to stall cleanly for one cycle. This knowledge prevents subtle timing errors. Fourth, you will analyze how forwarding changes CPI and how frequent load-use pairs still raise CPI. Together these objectives prepare you to implement and reason about forwarding in hardware or to test it in simulation.

screens.title: What is forwarding (bypassing)?
screens.narratorSegment: Forwarding is the hardware technique that routes a computed result from a later pipeline stage directly into an earlier stage so a dependent instruction can use it without waiting for register writeback. In practical terms, the ALU input multiplexers can select the ALU result stored in the EX over the value read from the register file. The motivation is simple: raw writeback timing imposes artificial stalls when a later instruction produces a value needed immediately. A concrete example makes this clear. Consider an add that writes R1 followed by a subtract that uses R1 as a source. Without forwarding the subtract must wait until the add's writeback completes. With forwarding, the add's ALU result is routed into the subtract's ALU input and the subtract proceeds without an extra cycle. A useful mental model is an express lane that bypasses the slower register-file lane. A common misconception is that forwarding removes all stalls; it does not. The load-use case still forces a one-cycle bubble because load data becomes available only at the end of memory. Keep that limitation in mind as you design your selects. Now try to describe in words how you would wire a multiplexer to choose between register file data and a forwarded ALU result.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Forwarding routes results from pipeline registers to ALU inputs so dependent instructions can proceed without waiting for register file writeback.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › What is Forwarding?
Forwarding explained
Route results directly to where they are needed to avoid waiting for writeback.
Definition
Select ALU or memory output from a pipeline register instead of the register file when a source register matches a recently written destination.
Concrete example
ADD writes R1, immediately followed by SUB that reads R1. Forward the ADD's ALU result into the SUB's ALU input so the SUB does not stall.
Common misconception
Forwarding does not remove load-use hazards because load data is only ready at the end of the memory stage, too late for the dependent instruction in EX.
Key takeaway
Forwarding is the express lane that greatly reduces RAW stalls, but it is not universal — loads still force stalls.
Analogy
Think of the register file as a busy toll bridge. Forwarding is a dedicated highway exit that lets a recent result bypass the toll and arrive sooner.
Try this
Sketch a single ALU input multiplexer and label the three inputs you expect to choose from in later slides.

screens.title: The three forwarding paths
screens.narratorSegment: There are three forwarding paths in the five-stage pipeline that cover most data hazards. First, EX/MEM to EX — this is often called Forward A — forwards the ALU result from the instruction currently in the EX or EX/MEM register into the ALU input of the next instruction. It is used when the previous instruction writes the register the current instruction reads. The enabling condition is that the EX/MEM pipeline register asserts a write enable and its destination register equals the EX stage source register. Second, MEM/WB to EX — Forward B — supplies a result produced by the instruction two cycles earlier. The enabling condition is similar but checks the MEM/WB write enable and destination against the EX source. Third, MEM/WB to MEM — Forward C — is used for stores: if a store instruction needs a value loaded by a prior load, the value in MEM/WB is forwarded into the memory write data input during the store's MEM stage. A common pitfall is thinking MEM/WB can resolve the load-use hazard for an immediate successor; it cannot because the dependent instruction needs the value earlier in EX. Remember the forwarding unit chooses EX/MEM first if both match, because it represents the most recent result.

keyIdea.title: Forwarding paths
keyIdea.text: EX/MEM→EX handles the immediately preceding instruction, MEM/WB→EX handles two-cycles-earlier results, and MEM/WB→MEM supports store data forwarding.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Forwarding Paths
Three forwarding paths
Step-by-step conditions and use cases
1. EX/MEM → EX (Forward A)
When the instruction in EX/MEM will write a register and that destination matches the EX instruction's source, forward the ALU result into EX ALU input.
2. MEM/WB → EX (Forward B)
When the instruction in MEM/WB will write a register and its destination matches the EX source, forward the value from MEM/WB into EX ALU input.
3. MEM/WB → MEM (Forward C)
For a store instruction needing a value that was just loaded, forward MEM/WB data into the memory write-data input during MEM.
Misconception check
MEM/WB cannot always resolve use by the immediately following instruction because timing may be too late for EX.
Visual summary
Three compact cards below show direction and typical source data.
EX/MEM → EX
Source: ALU result in EX/MEM. Destination: ALU input in EX.
MEM/WB → EX
Source: value in MEM/WB (ALU or loaded memory). Destination: ALU input in EX.
MEM/WB → MEM
Source: MEM/WB. Destination: memory write-data for a store instruction in MEM stage.
Key takeaway
These three paths cover most RAW dependencies in a five-stage pipeline; implement them with multiplexers and comparator-based selects.

screens.title: ALU input multiplexers and select signals
screens.narratorSegment: The ALU has two inputs and each input must choose among three sources: the register file value, the EX/MEM pipeline register, or the MEM/WB pipeline register. To support those choices implement a small multiplexer for each ALU operand. The hazard detection unit drives select bits that tell the multiplexer whether to pick the register file or one of the forwarded values. A typical encoding uses two select bits per input: no forwarding is 00, forward from EX/MEM is 01, and forward from MEM/WB is 10. Remember the priority: if both EX/MEM and MEM/WB match the same source, EX/MEM is chosen because it contains the most recent result. Practically, you will compare the EX/MEM. Rd and MEM/WB. Rd fields with the ID/EX source fields and also check that the write enable signals are asserted and that the destination register is not zero. This architecture keeps forwarding logic small, predictable, and local to the EX stage, while the comparators live in the hazard unit. ALU input multiplexers and select signals means each alu input uses a 3-way multiplexer selected by hazard unit logic: 00 = regfile, 01 = ex/mem, 10 = mem/wb; ex/mem has priority.. In practical terms, how alu inputs choose register file or forwarded data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › ALU Multiplexers
ALU input selection
Each ALU operand chooses among three sources using two select bits.
Select encoding
00 = register file, 01 = EX/MEM, 10 = MEM/WB. EX/MEM takes priority when both could match.
Comparator inputs
Compare destination register fields in EX/MEM and MEM/WB with the EX stage source fields, and ensure RegWrite is asserted and Rd is not zero.
Practical note
Keep forwarding decisions local to the EX stage; only the hazard unit needs visibility into pipeline register fields to drive selects.
Illustration
A compact diagram: ALU input multiplexer accepts RegFile, EX/MEM data, MEM/WB data. Hazard unit supplies select bits for each input.
Key takeaway
Design simple two-bit selects per ALU input and centralize comparator logic in the hazard unit for clarity and priority enforcement.

screens.title: ForwardA and ForwardB logic
screens.narratorSegment: The forwarding unit implements two main outputs commonly called ForwardA and ForwardB, one for each ALU operand. The logic checks the destination register in the EX/MEM stage first and uses it when RegWrite is asserted and the destination is not register zero. If that does not match, it checks the MEM/WB stage. This ordering enforces the priority that the most recent computed value is used. Expressed compactly, ForwardA selects EX/MEM if EX/MEM. RegWrite and EX/MEM. Rd is nonzero and equals the EX stage Rs1; otherwise select MEM/WB when MEM/WB. RegWrite and MEM/WB. Rd is nonzero and equals Rs1; otherwise no forwarding. ForwardB follows the same pattern comparing to Rs2. A subtle point is that Rd == 0 should be ignored because register zero is not writable. Another subtlety is whether MEM/WB forwards ALU results or loaded memory data; the hazard unit does not need to distinguish here — MEM/WB carries the correct value to forward. Finally, always test the logic with sequences where both EX/MEM and MEM/WB target the same register so you confirm the priority behavior. ForwardA and ForwardB logic means forwarda and forwardb compare ex/mem and mem/wb destination registers to ex source registers, prioritizing ex/mem when both match.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › ForwardA / ForwardB Logic
Comparator rules
Priority to EX/MEM, then MEM/WB; ignore register zero.
Behavior
Check EX/MEM first. If it matches and writes a nonzero destination, forward from EX/MEM. Else, if MEM/WB matches and writes, forward from MEM/WB. Else use register file.
Subtle checks
Always require the write-enable signal and that the destination register is not zero to avoid false matches and incorrect forwarding.
Pseudocode (visual)
ForwardA =
  if (EX/MEM.RegWrite and EX/MEM.Rd != 0 and EX/MEM.Rd == ID/EX.Rs1) then 01
  else if (MEM/WB.RegWrite and MEM/WB.Rd != 0 and MEM/WB.Rd == ID/EX.Rs1) then 10
  else 00

ForwardB =
  if (EX/MEM.RegWrite and EX/MEM.Rd != 0 and EX/MEM.Rd == ID/EX.Rs2) then 01
  else if (MEM/WB.RegWrite and MEM/WB.Rd != 0 and MEM/WB.Rd == ID/EX.Rs2) then 10
  else 00
Test idea
Run a sequence where two previous instructions write the same register to confirm EX/MEM forwarding wins over MEM/WB.

screens.title: Why EX/MEM forwarding has priority
screens.narratorSegment: The hazard unit prioritizes EX/MEM forwarding over MEM/WB forwarding because EX/MEM holds the result from the most recent preceding instruction in program order. If two earlier instructions write the same register, the later one must be the source of truth. Consider the small sequence: an ADD writes R1, then a SUB writes R1, followed by an AND that reads R1. In this case the SUB is the most recent writer and its result should reach the AND. If the hazard unit mistakenly used the older ADD result from MEM/WB, correctness fails. The comparator logic checks EX/MEM first, and only if that stage does not match will it consider MEM/WB. A common student error is to test both matches independently and choose MEM/WB in hardware without enforcing priority. Always write the logic as a cascade so EX/MEM short-circuits selection when matching. This rule guarantees that forwarding respects program order and avoids stale values being used. Reflect on how you would verify this property in simulation. Why EX/MEM forwarding has priority means ex/mem is prioritized because it holds the most recent write; using it prevents stale values from being forwarded when two prior writes target the same register.. In practical terms, understanding recent-result precedence with an example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Priority: EX/MEM over MEM/WB
Priority explained
Recent writes must be observed first to preserve program order.
Example sequence
ADD writes R1; SUB writes R1; AND reads R1. AND must use SUB's result, which is in EX/MEM, not ADD's result in MEM/WB.
Wrong implementation
Choosing MEM/WB blindly when both match returns a stale value and breaks correctness. Always check EX/MEM first.
Verification tip
Simulate a case with two writers to one register and inspect which pipeline register supplies the forwarded value to the dependent instruction.
Test scenario
Use the sequence: ADD R1,R2,R3; SUB R1,R4,R5; AND R6,R1,R7. Confirm AND receives SUB's result via EX/MEM forwarding and not ADD's via MEM/WB.
Key takeaway
Priority is a correctness requirement: newer writes supersede older ones when forwarding decisions overlap.

screens.title: Load-use hazard: why forwarding fails
screens.narratorSegment: The load-use hazard is the primary limitation of forwarding. A load instruction obtains its data from memory at the end of the MEM stage. A dependent instruction that immediately follows needs that data at the start of its EX stage, which arrives one half-cycle or cycle too late for use even with forwarding. The effect is simple: forwarding cannot make the data available earlier because the data is produced only after memory access completes. The classic sequence demonstrates this: a load writes R1 in MEM/WB after MEM finishes; the next instruction is an add that needs R1 in EX. Forwarding from MEM/WB to EX arrives too late for that add; you must stall for one cycle. Implementation-wise, the hazard detection unit checks if the instruction in ID/EX is a memory read and whether its destination matches the source registers of the instruction in IF/ID; when true assert Stall, hold ID, prevent IF advance, and insert a bubble into EX. A frequent student misconception is thinking MEM/WB forwarding handles this; emphasize that the timing of the load result prevents that. Consider how compilers can sometimes schedule an independent instruction into the delay slot to avoid the stall.

keyIdea.title: Load-use hazard
keyIdea.text: Loads produce data at end of MEM, too late for an immediate successor's EX stage; a one-cycle stall (bubble) is required.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Load-use Hazard
Why forwarding can't fix load-use
A timing mismatch between memory and EX stage forces a stall.
Concrete example
LW R1,0(R2) followed immediately by ADD R3,R1,R4. The load's data arrives only at end of MEM; ADD needs it at start of EX, so a stall is required.
Hazard detection
When the ID/EX stage indicates a memory read and its destination equals the next instruction's source, assert Stall, hold ID, prevent fetching, and insert a bubble into EX.
Common mitigation

screens.title: Stalling mechanism and bubble insertion
screens.narratorSegment: When the hazard detection unit recognizes a load-use pattern it must stall the pipeline for one cycle and insert a bubble. The detection condition checks whether the instruction in the decode-execute register is a memory read and whether its destination register matches either source register of the instruction in fetch-decode. If true, the control signals to the EX stage are set to a no-operation, the ID stage is held so its instruction does not advance, and the IF stage is prevented from fetching the next instruction. Practically implement this by asserting a Stall signal, gating the PC update, and replacing the ID/EX pipeline register contents that would move into EX with a NOP encoding. This ensures the instruction behind the load does not use incorrect or stale data. A common implementation detail is to keep the control signals stable in ID while inserting the bubble into EX. Test this by stepping through cycles to confirm the load's data reaches MEM, the bubble occupies EX for one cycle, and the dependent instruction proceeds in the following cycle with correct forwarded or register data.

Stall sequence
Detect load-use, hold ID, prevent IF, insert NOP into EX for one cycle.
Detection condition
If the ID/EX stage is a memory read and its destination equals IF/ID source registers then Stall = 1 and insert bubble.
Pipeline control
Gate the program counter update, hold ID/EX input latches, and write NOP control signals into EX stage for one cycle to create the bubble.
Cycle-by-cycle illustration
Cycle N: load in ID/EX (MemRead asserted). Cycle N+1: Stall asserted, bubble in EX, dependent instruction remains in ID. Cycle N+2: dependent enters EX with data available.

screens.title: How forwarding changes CPI
screens.narratorSegment: Forwarding dramatically reduces the CPI penalty for read-after-write hazards by supplying values directly to dependent instructions. Without forwarding a RAW hazard typically costs two stall cycles because the dependent instruction must wait for writeback. With forwarding most RAW hazards cost zero extra cycles because the forwarding paths supply the needed value into EX. Empirical numbers from the chapter show a typical CPI drop from around 1.5 without forwarding to roughly 1.1 to 1.2 with forwarding enabled. However, load-use pairs still cost one extra cycle each. If a workload has many successive loads followed immediately by uses — such as pointer-chasing workloads — those load-use stalls dominate and push CPI higher. To quantify, count the fraction of instructions that are load-use pairs and add one cycle per occurrence to the baseline CPI computed with forwarding. When analyzing performance, separate the effect of forwarding on ALU-ALU dependencies from the residual cost of memory dependencies; this separation helps identify whether compiler or microarchitecture optimizations will be most effective. How forwarding changes CPI means forwarding reduces raw stalls dramatically, lowering cpi from about 1.5 to near 1.1–1.2 on typical workloads; load-use pairs still add one cycle each.. In practical terms, quantify stall reduction and the remaining cost of loads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Performance Impact
Quantifying the benefit
Forwarding removes most RAW stalls; loads remain costly.
Typical numbers
Without forwarding a pipeline may see a CPI near 1.5 from RAW stalls. With forwarding this can drop to about 1.1–1.2 for many workloads.
Effect of load-use pairs
Each load-use pair still costs an extra cycle. If such pairs are frequent, they add significantly to CPI even with forwarding.
Analysis method
Estimate baseline CPI with forwarding, then add the frequency of load-use pairs times one cycle to compute expected CPI for your workload.
Practical example
If forwarding reduces RAW stalls to give CPI = 1.12 and your code has 5% load-use pairs, approximate CPI = 1.12 + 0.05 * 1 = 1.17.
Key takeaway
Forwarding brings large gains, but measuring load-use frequency is essential to predict real CPI for memory-heavy code.

screens.title: Reducing load-use stalls
screens.narratorSegment: Although forwarding cannot remove the load-use stall itself, several techniques reduce how often it happens. Compiler scheduling is the simplest: the compiler can insert an independent instruction between a load and its use to fill the one-cycle delay slot. This requires the compiler to find useful instructions that do not depend on the loaded value. Microarchitectural approaches include out-of-order execution, which allows other independent instructions to execute while the load completes, and speculative load execution or value prediction, which guess the loaded value to keep dependent instructions moving. Another approach is load-store optimization: the compiler or runtime can reorder loads and stores to separate loads from their uses. Each technique comes with trade-offs: compiler scheduling is low overhead but limited by available independent work; out-of-order hardware increases complexity and power; value prediction risks mis-speculation. When analyzing a design, consider whether reducing load-use frequency through software is sufficient or whether hardware support is justified by workload characteristics. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Reducing Load-Use Stalls
Strategies and trade-offs
Practical techniques to lower the frequency of load-use penalties.
Compiler scheduling
Insert independent instructions between a load and its use to hide the one-cycle delay. Low cost but depends on available independent work.
Out-of-order execution
Hardware can execute other ready instructions while a load waits, reducing the visible stall count for the program at higher complexity and power cost.
Speculation & value prediction
Speculatively execute dependent instructions or predict the loaded value to proceed; mispredictions require recovery and cost extra cycles.
Decision guide
Choose a mitigation based on workload: compilers for simple gains, out-of-order or speculation for heavy memory-latency workloads where complexity is justified.
Key takeaway
No single method eliminates load-use cost in an in-order pipeline; combine compiler and microarchitectural approaches as appropriate.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we study forwarding, also called bypassing, and the hazard logic that makes it work. Forwarding is the technique that lets an instruction use a result before that result is written back to the register file. That simple idea reduces pipeline stalls dramatically in an in-order five-stage pipeline. You will see the three forwarding paths commonly implemented, the multiplexers that choose forwarded data instead of the register file, and the comparator logic the hazard unit uses to decide when to forward. We will also cover the key exception — the load-use hazard — which cannot be eliminated by forwarding and requires a one-cycle stall. Along the way you will learn why the unit prioritizes the more recent pipeline stage when both stages could forward, and how forwarding changes typical CPI numbers for realistic code. This chapter is practical: it prepares you to design the forwarding multiplexers and the hazard detection logic, to detect load-use cases, and to reason about where stalls remain. Think about forwarding as express highways that let values bypass the register file and arrive at the ALU earlier. Why is that optimization so important in pipelined processors?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement forwarding paths in a five-stage datapath, design the hazard detection unit, explain the load-use limitation, and analyze the performance impact. First, implementing forwarding paths means identifying the ALU inputs that can accept bypassed values and wiring multiplexers to the EX/MEM and MEM/WB pipeline registers. That skill matters because it removes many read-after-write stalls and improves throughput. Second, designing the hazard detection unit requires writing the compare logic that sets those multiplexer selects and enforces priority. Understanding this logic ensures correctness when two previous instructions write the same register. Third, you will learn why forwarding cannot resolve load-use hazards and how to stall cleanly for one cycle. This knowledge prevents subtle timing errors. Fourth, you will analyze how forwarding changes CPI and how frequent load-use pairs still raise CPI. Together these objectives prepare you to implement and reason about forwarding in hardware or to test it in simulation.

This second objectives slide drills into the practical outputs you will produce. You will implement three forwarding paths: the EX/MEM to EX path for the immediately preceding instruction, the MEM/WB to EX path for the instruction two cycles earlier, and the MEM/WB to MEM path to support store writes. For each path you will specify the correct source, destination, and the conditions under which forwarding is enabled. You will write the forwarding multiplexer selects and the hazard comparator logic using clear priority rules so that the most recent result is chosen when two writebacks target the same register. You will also instrument a simple test sequence to show which forward path is used for each dependency and to measure cycles with and without forwarding. These concrete artifacts let you validate and reason about the single-cycle load-use stall and the overall CPI effect.

Forwarding is the hardware technique that routes a computed result from a later pipeline stage directly into an earlier stage so a dependent instruction can use it without waiting for register writeback. In practical terms, the ALU input multiplexers can select the ALU result stored in the EX over the value read from the register file. The motivation is simple: raw writeback timing imposes artificial stalls when a later instruction produces a value needed immediately. A concrete example makes this clear. Consider an add that writes R1 followed by a subtract that uses R1 as a source. Without forwarding the subtract must wait until the add's writeback completes. With forwarding, the add's ALU result is routed into the subtract's ALU input and the subtract proceeds without an extra cycle. A useful mental model is an express lane that bypasses the slower register-file lane. A common misconception is that forwarding removes all stalls; it does not. The load-use case still forces a one-cycle bubble because load data becomes available only at the end of memory. Keep that limitation in mind as you design your selects. Now try to describe in words how you would wire a multiplexer to choose between register file data and a forwarded ALU result.

There are three forwarding paths in the five-stage pipeline that cover most data hazards. First, EX/MEM to EX — this is often called Forward A — forwards the ALU result from the instruction currently in the EX or EX/MEM register into the ALU input of the next instruction. It is used when the previous instruction writes the register the current instruction reads. The enabling condition is that the EX/MEM pipeline register asserts a write enable and its destination register equals the EX stage source register. Second, MEM/WB to EX — Forward B — supplies a result produced by the instruction two cycles earlier. The enabling condition is similar but checks the MEM/WB write enable and destination against the EX source. Third, MEM/WB to MEM — Forward C — is used for stores: if a store instruction needs a value loaded by a prior load, the value in MEM/WB is forwarded into the memory write data input during the store's MEM stage. A common pitfall is thinking MEM/WB can resolve the load-use hazard for an immediate successor; it cannot because the dependent instruction needs the value earlier in EX. Remember the forwarding unit chooses EX/MEM first if both match, because it represents the most recent result.

The ALU has two inputs and each input must choose among three sources: the register file value, the EX/MEM pipeline register, or the MEM/WB pipeline register. To support those choices implement a small multiplexer for each ALU operand. The hazard detection unit drives select bits that tell the multiplexer whether to pick the register file or one of the forwarded values. A typical encoding uses two select bits per input: no forwarding is 00, forward from EX/MEM is 01, and forward from MEM/WB is 10. Remember the priority: if both EX/MEM and MEM/WB match the same source, EX/MEM is chosen because it contains the most recent result. Practically, you will compare the EX/MEM. Rd and MEM/WB. Rd fields with the ID/EX source fields and also check that the write enable signals are asserted and that the destination register is not zero. This architecture keeps forwarding logic small, predictable, and local to the EX stage, while the comparators live in the hazard unit. ALU input multiplexers and select signals means each alu input uses a 3-way multiplexer selected by hazard unit logic: 00 = regfile, 01 = ex/mem, 10 = mem/wb; ex/mem has priority.. In practical terms, how alu inputs choose register file or forwarded data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The forwarding unit implements two main outputs commonly called ForwardA and ForwardB, one for each ALU operand. The logic checks the destination register in the EX/MEM stage first and uses it when RegWrite is asserted and the destination is not register zero. If that does not match, it checks the MEM/WB stage. This ordering enforces the priority that the most recent computed value is used. Expressed compactly, ForwardA selects EX/MEM if EX/MEM. RegWrite and EX/MEM. Rd is nonzero and equals the EX stage Rs1; otherwise select MEM/WB when MEM/WB. RegWrite and MEM/WB. Rd is nonzero and equals Rs1; otherwise no forwarding. ForwardB follows the same pattern comparing to Rs2. A subtle point is that Rd == 0 should be ignored because register zero is not writable. Another subtlety is whether MEM/WB forwards ALU results or loaded memory data; the hazard unit does not need to distinguish here — MEM/WB carries the correct value to forward. Finally, always test the logic with sequences where both EX/MEM and MEM/WB target the same register so you confirm the priority behavior. ForwardA and ForwardB logic means forwarda and forwardb compare ex/mem and mem/wb destination registers to ex source registers, prioritizing ex/mem when both match.. In practical terms, comparator rules and priority explained with code-like pseudocode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The hazard unit prioritizes EX/MEM forwarding over MEM/WB forwarding because EX/MEM holds the result from the most recent preceding instruction in program order. If two earlier instructions write the same register, the later one must be the source of truth. Consider the small sequence: an ADD writes R1, then a SUB writes R1, followed by an AND that reads R1. In this case the SUB is the most recent writer and its result should reach the AND. If the hazard unit mistakenly used the older ADD result from MEM/WB, correctness fails. The comparator logic checks EX/MEM first, and only if that stage does not match will it consider MEM/WB. A common student error is to test both matches independently and choose MEM/WB in hardware without enforcing priority. Always write the logic as a cascade so EX/MEM short-circuits selection when matching. This rule guarantees that forwarding respects program order and avoids stale values being used. Reflect on how you would verify this property in simulation. Why EX/MEM forwarding has priority means ex/mem is prioritized because it holds the most recent write; using it prevents stale values from being forwarded when two prior writes target the same register.. In practical terms, understanding recent-result precedence with an example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The load-use hazard is the primary limitation of forwarding. A load instruction obtains its data from memory at the end of the MEM stage. A dependent instruction that immediately follows needs that data at the start of its EX stage, which arrives one half-cycle or cycle too late for use even with forwarding. The effect is simple: forwarding cannot make the data available earlier because the data is produced only after memory access completes. The classic sequence demonstrates this: a load writes R1 in MEM/WB after MEM finishes; the next instruction is an add that needs R1 in EX. Forwarding from MEM/WB to EX arrives too late for that add; you must stall for one cycle. Implementation-wise, the hazard detection unit checks if the instruction in ID/EX is a memory read and whether its destination matches the source registers of the instruction in IF/ID; when true assert Stall, hold ID, prevent IF advance, and insert a bubble into EX. A frequent student misconception is thinking MEM/WB forwarding handles this; emphasize that the timing of the load result prevents that. Consider how compilers can sometimes schedule an independent instruction into the delay slot to avoid the stall.

When the hazard detection unit recognizes a load-use pattern it must stall the pipeline for one cycle and insert a bubble. The detection condition checks whether the instruction in the decode-execute register is a memory read and whether its destination register matches either source register of the instruction in fetch-decode. If true, the control signals to the EX stage are set to a no-operation, the ID stage is held so its instruction does not advance, and the IF stage is prevented from fetching the next instruction. Practically implement this by asserting a Stall signal, gating the PC update, and replacing the ID/EX pipeline register contents that would move into EX with a NOP encoding. This ensures the instruction behind the load does not use incorrect or stale data. A common implementation detail is to keep the control signals stable in ID while inserting the bubble into EX. Test this by stepping through cycles to confirm the load's data reaches MEM, the bubble occupies EX for one cycle, and the dependent instruction proceeds in the following cycle with correct forwarded or register data.

Forwarding dramatically reduces the CPI penalty for read-after-write hazards by supplying values directly to dependent instructions. Without forwarding a RAW hazard typically costs two stall cycles because the dependent instruction must wait for writeback. With forwarding most RAW hazards cost zero extra cycles because the forwarding paths supply the needed value into EX. Empirical numbers from the chapter show a typical CPI drop from around 1.5 without forwarding to roughly 1.1 to 1.2 with forwarding enabled. However, load-use pairs still cost one extra cycle each. If a workload has many successive loads followed immediately by uses — such as pointer-chasing workloads — those load-use stalls dominate and push CPI higher. To quantify, count the fraction of instructions that are load-use pairs and add one cycle per occurrence to the baseline CPI computed with forwarding. When analyzing performance, separate the effect of forwarding on ALU-ALU dependencies from the residual cost of memory dependencies; this separation helps identify whether compiler or microarchitecture optimizations will be most effective. Although forwarding cannot remove the load-use stall itself, several techniques reduce how often it happens. Compiler scheduling is the simplest: the compiler can insert an independent instruction between a load and its use to fill the one-cycle delay slot. This requires the compiler to find useful instructions that do not depend on the loaded value. Microarchitectural approaches include out-of-order execution, which allows other independent instructions to execute while the load completes, and speculative load execution or value prediction, which guess the loaded value to keep dependent instructions moving. Another approach is load-store optimization: the compiler or runtime can reorder loads and stores to separate loads from their uses. Each technique comes with trade-offs: compiler scheduling is low overhead but limited by available independent work; out-of-order hardware increases complexity and power; value prediction risks mis-speculation. When analyzing a design, consider whether reducing load-use frequency through software is sufficient or whether hardware support is justified by workload characteristics. These six compact concepts summarize the chapter. Forwarding paths include EX/MEM to EX, MEM/WB to EX, and MEM/WB to MEM. ALU inputs use multiplexers to select register file data or forwarded values; the hazard unit generates the select signals. The hazard detection logic compares destination registers in later pipeline stages with EX stage sources and enforces EX/MEM priority over MEM/WB so the most recent write is used. Load-use hazards remain an exception: loads produce data too late for an immediate successor, so a one-cycle stall with a bubble is required. Finally, forwarding greatly reduces RAW stalls and lowers CPI from roughly 1.5 to about 1.1–1.2 on many workloads, but frequent load-use pairs still add cycles. Keep these points in mind when you design or verify a forwarding and hazard-detection unit.
